title: Kindergarten goodbyes: tears are not adjustment failure, but proof of trust
dek: One child is rated a ‘leader’ by teachers yet cries daily at drop-off; another excels at ‘playing the good kid’ and collapses at home. Same root cause: children carry weight at school and only unload it at home.
why: No new research, no expert theories—just detailed analysis of two real parent letters. For parents navigating the anxiety of school adaptation and wondering whether to change schools.
who: Parents navigating their children's school-entry anxiety, wondering whether difficulties stem from personality or poor school fit—especially those with ‘perfectionist’ or ‘emotional sponge’ children.
skip: Commercial insurance ad segments that appear repeatedly in the letters can be skipped; they contain no substantive content.

points.h: A quiet classroom doesn't signal unhappiness or poor fit
points.body: The mother observed her daughter's kindergarten classroom was much quieter than preschool, with children sitting still on a mat rather than on her lap and chiming in. She worried the emphasis on obedience sacrificed classroom joy. Janet acknowledges this is a common gap between preschool and kindergarten, but explains it doesn't signal poor adjustment. The teacher and principal both describe the daughter as a ‘leader’—evidence she's thriving, not being crushed by the environment.

points.h: Perfectionist children naturally feel sharper school-entry pressure
points.body: Janet observes that only children or eldest daughters who are high-achievers often want to ‘slide elegantly’ into new environments. They don't want to visibly struggle or be in learning mode; they want to get it right immediately. This personality naturally amplifies the normal stress of adaptation. But it's not evidence the environment is wrong for them—just that this temperament inherently feels the pressure more sharply.

points.h: She asks: ‘Will anyone notice I'm crying?’
points.body: Before crying at the gate, the daughter sings a song and performs a ‘kiss hand’ goodbye ritual. The moment she starts crying, she wipes her tears immediately and asks ‘Can I cry for a bit?’, then ‘Do I look okay now? Can I go in?’ Janet finds this detail crucial: the child is already worried that showing vulnerability will get her blamed by teachers. This worry itself reveals how hard she's trying to live up to the ‘leader’ role.

points.h: Tears are not adjustment failure, but her doing what's right
points.body: Janet shares her own habit of crying before major speeches. The first time it surprised her, but she found that crying made her feel better and allowed her to show up vulnerable and human to her audience. She urges the mother to go further than just ‘allowing’ tears: actively tell the daughter that crying feels good, nobody minds if she walks in with wet cheeks, and in fact others will connect with her more authentically.

points.h: Goodbye rituals are lovely, but may mask real anxiety
points.body: Janet raises a caution: the mother's pre-gate singing and intimate goodbye gesture are beautiful, but warrant honest self-examination. If they're meant to ‘gloss over’ her own hidden doubts about the school rather than simply celebrate love, the child can see through it. Janet stresses that children always sense our true feelings; the parent must first feel genuinely settled about the environment herself.

points.h: Playing the good kid at school exacts a home-life cost
points.body: A six-year-old boy is praised by teachers as well-behaved and thoughtful. But at home he spits, shrieks, destroys his older siblings' things, and resists bath time and bed. His parents suspect he's so hard on himself at school to compensate for the chaos created by classmates with special needs who get lots of negative attention. At school he plays ‘good child’; at home he has nowhere for that stress.

points.h: He's absorbing others' emotions, not falling apart himself
points.body: Janet reframes the boy's behavior. He's processing and venting the struggles he witnesses from other children in the classroom; he's a sensitive, empathetic child absorbing their emotions and even mimicking their specific behaviors, then needing to expel it all at home. This isn't ordinary meltdown—it's the accumulated cost of playing ‘school's good kid’ while carrying others' weight.

points.h: ‘I know I don't want to, but I can't stop’
points.body: When the boy expresses that he knows he doesn't want to behave this way, and in calm moments says the same thing, but admits he doesn't know how to stop, Janet sees this as a sign of safety and trust in the parent relationship. The parent's job isn't to find him an answer but to stay curious and keep asking what's happening at school, so he knows his parents truly have his back.

quotes.text: This morning as she began crying at drop-off, she quietly asked me whether it was okay to cry for a little while, and then whether it was obvious to others that she was upset. That particularly stayed with me.
What I've noticed is that when she starts crying at drop-off, she immediately tries to wipe away her own tears. She follows this by asking if it's okay if she cries a bit.
And crying is not only okay, it's the best thing that she could do right there. I really believe that.

It made me feel so much better just to let that out. It really allowed me to feel okay, whatever, I'm vulnerable, I'm going to go in open as myself, connecting with people on a human level that way, showing them my humanity.
I know he does not want to be acting this way, and he will say as much in calmer moments, but he also said he does not know how to stop himself.
I mean, how beautiful is that, that he can articulate that and know that. That's a testament to his relationship with his parents and the safety that he feels in sharing what a struggle is.
